final_proof:
As written, the claim is false: without a topology on X, the usual topological meaning of “discrete family” is not even defined.

For a counterexample under the usual meaning, give X={0,1} the indiscrete topology and the well-order 0≺1, and put V_k=Δ_X for every k≥0. Every V_k contains Δ_X and is symmetric, while V_k∘V_k=Δ_X⊆V_{k-1} for k>0. Thus all the stated relation hypotheses hold. Moreover, U_k=Δ_X, so for every k>0,

A_k(0)={0},  and  A_k(1)={1}\setminus{0}={1}.

Hence 𝒜_k={{0},{1}}. In the indiscrete topology the only neighborhood of either point is X, which meets both members of 𝒜_k. Therefore 𝒜_k is not discrete.

The corrected result is obtained by assuming that X is a topological space and that, for every k≥1 and p∈X, the section

V_k[p]={q∈X:(p,q)∈V_k}

is a neighborhood of p. Under this additional hypothesis, every 𝒜_n is discrete.

Proof. Use the convention (S∘R)[x]=S[R[x]]. Fix n≥1 and p∈X. We show that the neighborhood V_{n+2}[p] meets at most one member of 𝒜_n.

Suppose that it meets both A_n(x) and A_n(y). Choose

a∈V_{n+2}[p]∩A_n(x),  b∈V_{n+2}[p]∩A_n(y).

If x≠y, totality of the well-order allows us, after interchanging x,y and a,b if necessary, to assume x≺y. Since V_{n+2} is symmetric, (p,a),(p,b)∈V_{n+2} imply (a,p),(p,b)∈V_{n+2}. Therefore

(a,b)∈V_{n+2}∘V_{n+2}⊆V_{n+1}.

Also a∈A_n(x)⊆U_n[x]. Consequently,

b∈V_{n+1}[U_n[x]]=(V_{n+1}∘U_n)[x]=U_{n+1}[x],

where the last equality follows from associativity of relation composition and U_j=V_j∘⋯∘V_1. But x≺y, so U_{n+1}[x] is among the sets removed in

A_n(y)=U_n[y]\setminus⋃_{z≼y, z≠y}U_{n+1}[z].

Thus b∉A_n(y), contradicting the choice of b. Hence x=y, proving that V_{n+2}[p] meets at most one member of 𝒜_n.

By the added hypothesis, V_{n+2}[p] is a neighborhood of p. Since p was arbitrary, every point has a neighborhood meeting at most one member of 𝒜_n; hence 𝒜_n is discrete. Since n was arbitrary, this holds for every n>0.
